Temporary credentials cannot be extended or refreshed beyond the original specified interval.

When you make a call using temporary security credentials, the call must include a session token, which is returned along with those temporary credentials. AWS uses the session token to validate the temporary security credentials.

This can reduce latency (server lag) by sending the requests to servers in a Region that is geographically closer to you. No matter which Region your credentials come from, they work globally.

claim: An instance profile is the container that passes a role to an EC2 instance; it can hold only one IAM role and this limit cannot be increased, only one role can be assigned to an instance at a time, and the application obtains the role's temporary credentials from the instance metadata without any stored keys.

Only one role can be assigned to an Amazon EC2 instance at a time, and all applications on the instance share the same role and permissions.

Applications, AWS CLI, and Tools for Windows PowerShell commands that run on the instance can then get automatic temporary security credentials from the instance metadata. You do not have to explicitly get the temporary security credentials.

The **IAM Role** list in the Amazon EC2 console lists the names of instance profiles, not the names of roles.

claim: Role credentials delivered to an EC2 instance are temporary and updated automatically, so you do not manage credentials on the instance; a change to a role shared by many instances propagates to all of them, and a role can be attached to an instance that is already running.

Although a role is usually assigned to an Amazon EC2 instance when you launch it, a role can also be attached to an Amazon EC2 instance currently running.

claim: To configure a service with a role, a user must have the iam:PassRole permission for that role; PassRole only works within the same account, and the role's trust policy must also allow the service to assume it.

the role's trust policy must also allow the service to assume it

evidence.quote: To pass a role (and its permissions) to an AWS service, a user must have permissions to *pass the role* to the service. This helps administrators ensure that only approved users can configure a service with a role that grants permissions. To allow a user to pass a role to an AWS service, you must grant the `PassRole` permission to the user's IAM user, role, or group.
You can only use the `PassRole` permission to pass an IAM role to a service that shares the same AWS account.
This trust policy allows Amazon EC2 to use the role and the permissions attached to the role.

claim: The PassRole check exists so that a user cannot pass a role with more permissions than the user should have; the user passes the role ARN in the API call and the service checks iam:PassRole, which you can limit to approved roles with the Resource element or to a service with the iam:PassedToService condition key.

values.display: a user cannot pass a role with more permissions than the user should have
the iam:PassedToService condition key

qualifiers.scope: passing a role to an AWS service

evidence.quote: When setting the `PassRole` permission, you should make sure that a user doesn’t pass a role where the role has more permissions than you want the user to have.

A user can pass a role ARN as a parameter in any API operation that uses the role to assign permissions to the service. The service then checks whether that user has the `iam:PassRole` permission. To limit the user to passing only approved roles, you can filter the `iam:PassRole` permission with the `Resources` element of the IAM policy statement.
The `iam:PassedToService` condition key can be used to specify the service principal of the service to which a role can be passed.

claim: A service role is a role that a service assumes to act on your behalf and that an IAM administrator can create, modify and delete; a service-linked role is a service role linked to one service, predefined by that service with permissions that only that service can assume and that cannot be attached to any other entity.

The linked service defines the permissions of its service-linked roles, and unless defined otherwise, only that service can assume the roles. The defined permissions include the trust policy and the permissions policy, and that permissions policy cannot be attached to any other IAM entity.

A service-linked role is a unique type of IAM role that is linked directly to an AWS service. Service-linked roles are predefined by the service and include all the permissions that the service requires to call other AWS services on your behalf.

claim: The confused deputy problem is when an entity without permission coerces a more privileged entity to act for it; for third-party cross-account access the external ID is an sts:ExternalId condition in the role's trust policy, generated and controlled by the third party and unique per customer, so the role can be assumed only when the AssumeRole call includes that value.

values.display: an entity without permission coerces a more privileged entity to act for it
an sts:ExternalId condition in the role's trust policy
generated and controlled by the third party and unique per customer

evidence.quote: The confused deputy problem is a security issue where an entity that doesn't have permission to perform an action can coerce a more-privileged entity to perform the action.

Example Corp can address the confused deputy problem by requiring that you include the `ExternalId` condition check in the role's trust policy. Example Corp generates a unique `ExternalId` value for each customer and uses that value in its request to assume the role. The `ExternalId` value must be unique among Example Corp's customers and controlled by Example Corp, not its customers.
The primary function of the external ID is to address and prevent [The confused deputy problem](confused-deputy.md).

You can't switch roles if you sign in as the AWS account root user.

claim: A managed policy is standalone and can be attached to many users, groups and roles, and AWS recommends managed policies in most cases; an inline policy is embedded in a single identity with a strict one-to-one relationship and is deleted with the identity.

a strict one-to-one relationship and is deleted with the identity

evidence.quote: An inline policy is a policy created for a single IAM identity (a user, user group, or role). Inline policies maintain a strict one-to-one relationship between a policy and an identity. They are deleted when you delete the identity.
A single managed policy can be attached to multiple principal entities (users, groups, and roles).
In most cases, we recommend that you use managed policies instead of inline policies.

IAM stores up to five versions of your customer managed policies. You can use policy versions to revert a policy to an earlier version as needed.
